{{Short description|Measure of the deviation of position over time}}
{{refimprove|date=January 2017}}

In [[statistical mechanics]], the '''mean squared displacement''' ('''MSD'''), also called '''mean square displacement''', '''average squared displacement''', or '''mean square fluctuation''', is a measure of the [[Deviation (statistics)|deviation]] of the [[position (geometry)|position]] of a [[particle]] with respect to a reference position over time. It is the most common measure of the spatial extent of random [[motion]], and can be thought of as measuring the portion of the system "explored" by the [[random walk]]er. 

In the realm of [[biophysics]] and [[environmental engineering]], the MSD is measured over time to determine if a particle is spreading slowly due to [[diffusion]], or if an [[Advection|advective]] force is also contributing.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Tarantino|first1=Nadine|last2=Tinevez|first2=Jean-Yves|last3=Crowell|first3=Elizabeth Faris|last4=Boisson|first4=Bertrand|last5=Henriques|first5=Ricardo|last6=Mhlanga|first6=Musa|last7=Agou|first7=Fabrice|last8=Israël|first8=Alain|last9=Laplantine|first9=Emmanuel|date=2014-01-20|title=TNF and IL-1 exhibit distinct ubiquitin requirements for inducing NEMO–IKK supramolecular structures|journal=J Cell Biol|language=en|volume=204|issue=2|pages=231–245|doi=10.1083/jcb.201307172|issn=0021-9525|pmc=3897181|pmid=24446482}}</ref> Another relevant concept, the '''variance-related diameter''' ('''VRD'''), defined as twice the [[square root]] of MSD, is also used in studying the transportation and mixing phenomena in [[environmental engineering]].<ref>{{Cite book|title=Mixing in inland and coastal waters|last=B.|first=Fischer, Hugo|date=1979-01-01|publisher=Academic Press|isbn=978-0-08-051177-1|oclc=983391285}}</ref> It prominently appears in the [[Debye–Waller factor]] (describing vibrations within the solid state) and in the [[Langevin equation]] (describing diffusion of a [[Brownian motion|Brownian particle]]). 

The MSD at time <math>t</math> is defined as an [[ensemble average]]:
<math display="block">\text{MSD} \equiv \left\langle \left|\mathbf{x}(t)-\mathbf{x_0}\right|^2\right\rangle
= \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \left|\mathbf{x^{(i)}}(t) - \mathbf{x^{(i)}}(0)\right|^2</math>
where ''N'' is the number of particles to be averaged, vector <math>\mathbf{x^{(i)}}(0)=\mathbf{x^{(i)}_0}</math> is the reference position of the <math>i</math>-th particle, and vector <math>\mathbf{x^{(i)}}(t)</math> is the position of the <math>i</math>-th particle at time ''t''.<ref>Frenkel, Daan & Smit, Berend. ''Understanding molecular simulation: From algorithms to applications''. Academic Press, 196 (2nd Ed.), p. 97.</ref>

==Derivation of the MSD for a Brownian particle in 1D==
The [[probability density function]] (PDF) for a particle in one dimension is found by solving the one-dimensional [[diffusion equation]]. (This equation states that the position probability density diffuses out over time - this is the method used by Einstein to describe a Brownian particle. Another method to describe the motion of a Brownian particle was described by Langevin, now known for its namesake as the [[Langevin equation]].)
<math display="block">
 \frac{\partial p(x, t \mid x_0)}{\partial t} = D\frac{\partial^2 p(x, t \mid x_0)}{\partial x^2},
</math>
given the initial condition <math>p(x,t=0 \mid x_0) = \delta(x - x_0)</math>; where <math>x(t)</math> is the position of the particle at some given time, <math>x_0</math> is the tagged particle's initial position, and <math>D</math> is the diffusion constant with the S.I. units <math>m^2s^{-1}</math> (an indirect measure of the particle's speed). The bar in the argument of the instantaneous probability refers to the [[conditional probability]]. The diffusion equation states that the speed at which the probability for finding the particle at <math>x(t)</math> is position dependent.

The [[differential equation]] above takes the form of 1D [[Heat equation#Fundamental solutions|heat equation]]. The one-dimensional PDF below is the [[Green's function]] of heat equation (also known as [[Heat kernel]] in mathematics):
<math display="block"> P(x,t) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi Dt}} \exp\left(-\frac{(x - x_0)^2}{4Dt}\right). </math>
This states that the probability of finding the particle at <math>x(t)</math> is Gaussian, and the width of the Gaussian is time dependent. More specifically the [[full width at half maximum]] (FWHM)(technically/pedantically, this is actually the Full ''duration'' at half maximum as the independent variable is time) scales like
<math display="block"> \text{FWHM}\sim\sqrt{t}. </math>
Using the PDF one is able to derive the average of a given function, <math>L</math>, at time <math>t</math>:
<math display="block"> \langle L(t) \rangle \equiv \int^\infty_{-\infty} L(x,t) P(x,t) \, dx, </math>
where the average is taken over all space (or any applicable variable).

The Mean squared displacement is defined as
<math display="block"> \text{MSD} \equiv \left\langle \left( x(t) - x_0 \right)^2 \right\rangle, </math>
expanding out the ensemble average
<math display="block"> \left\langle \left(x - x_0\right)^2 \right\rangle = \left\langle x^2 \right\rangle + x_0^2 - 2 x_0 \langle x \rangle, </math>
dropping the explicit time dependence notation for clarity. To find the MSD, one can take one of two paths: one can explicitly calculate <math>\langle x^2\rangle</math> and <math>\langle x\rangle</math>, then plug the result back into the definition of the MSD; or one could find the [[moment-generating function]], an extremely useful, and general function when dealing with probability densities. The moment-generating function describes the {{nowrap|<math>k</math>-th}} moment of the PDF. The first moment of the displacement PDF shown above is simply the mean: <math>\langle x\rangle</math>. The second moment is given as <math>\langle x^2\rangle</math>.

So then, to find the moment-generating function it is convenient to introduce the [[characteristic function (probability theory)|characteristic function]]:
<math display="block"> G(k) = \langle e^{ikx}\rangle\equiv \int_I e^{ikx}P(x,t\mid x_0) \, dx, </math>
one can expand out the exponential in the above equation to give
<math display="block"> G(k) = \sum^\infty_{m=0}\frac{(ik)^m}{m!}\mu_m. </math>
By taking the natural log of the characteristic function, a new function is produced, the [[cumulant generating function]],
<math display="block"> \ln(G(k)) = \sum^\infty_{m=1}\frac{(ik)^m}{m!}\kappa_m, </math>
where <math>\kappa_m</math> is the {{nowrap|<math>m</math>-th}} [[cumulant]] of <math>x</math>. The first two cumulants are related to the first two moments, <math>\mu</math>, via <math>\kappa_1 =\mu_1;</math> and <math>\kappa_2 =\mu_2-\mu_1^2,</math> where the second cumulant is the so-called variance, <math>\sigma^2</math>. With these definitions accounted for one can investigate the moments of the Brownian particle PDF,
<math display="block"> G(k) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi Dt}}\int_I \exp\left(i k x - \frac{\left(x - x_0\right)^2}{4Dt}\right) \, dx; </math>
by [[completing the square]] and knowing the total area under a Gaussian one arrives at
<math display="block"> G(k) = \exp(i k x_0 - k^2 D t). </math>
Taking the natural log, and comparing powers of <math>ik</math> to the cumulant generating function, the first cumulant is
<math display="block"> \kappa_1 = x_0, </math>
which is as expected, namely that the mean position is the Gaussian centre. The second cumulant is
<math display="block"> \kappa_2 = 2Dt, \,</math>
the factor 2 comes from the factorial factor in the denominator of the cumulant generating function. From this, the second moment is calculated,
<math display="block"> \mu_2 = \kappa_2 + \mu_1^2 = 2Dt + x_0^2. </math>
Plugging the results for the first and second moments back, one finds the MSD,
<math display="block"> \left\langle \left(x(t) - x_0\right)^2 \right\rangle = 2Dt. </math>

== Derivation for ''n'' dimensions ==
For a Brownian particle in higher-dimension [[Euclidean space]], its position is represented by a vector <math>\mathbf{x}=(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)</math>, where the [[Cartesian coordinate system|Cartesian coordinates]] <math>x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n</math> are [[Independence (probability theory)|statistically independent]].

The ''n''-variable probability distribution function is the product of the [[Heat equation#Fundamental solutions|fundamental solutions]] in each variable; i.e.,

<math display="block">P(\mathbf{x},t) = P(x_1,t)P(x_2,t)\dots P(x_n,t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{(4\pi D t)^n}}\exp \left (-\frac{\mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{x}}{4Dt} \right ).</math>

The Mean squared displacement is defined as

<math display="block">\mathrm{MSD} \equiv \left\langle |\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x_0}|^2\right\rangle
= \left\langle \left(x_1(t)-x_1(0)\right)^2 + \left(x_2(t)-x_2(0)\right)^2 + \dots + \left(x_n(t)-x_n(0)\right)^2 \right\rangle</math>

Since all the coordinates are independent, their deviation from the reference position is also independent. Therefore,

<math display="block"> \text{MSD}
= \left\langle \left(x_1(t)-x_1(0)\right)^2 \right\rangle + \left\langle \left(x_2(t)-x_2(0)\right)^2 \right\rangle + \dots + \left\langle \left(x_n(t)-x_n(0)\right)^2 \right\rangle</math>

For each coordinate, following the same derivation as in 1D scenario above, one obtains the MSD in that dimension as <math>
2Dt </math>. Hence, the final result of mean squared displacement in ''n''-dimensional Brownian motion is:

<math display="block"> \text{MSD} = 2nDt. </math>

==Definition of MSD for time lags==
In the measurements of single particle tracking (SPT), displacements can be defined for different time intervals between positions (also called time lags or lag times). SPT yields the trajectory <math>\vec r(t) = [x(t),y(t)]</math>, representing a particle undergoing two-dimensional diffusion. 

Assuming that the trajectory of a single particle measured at time points <math>1\,\Delta t, 2\,\Delta t,\ldots,N\,\Delta t</math>, where <math>\Delta t</math> is any fixed number, then there are <math>N(N-1)/2</math> non-trivial forward displacements <math>\vec d_{ij} = \vec r_j - \vec r_i</math> (<math>1 \leqslant i < j \leqslant N</math>, the cases when <math>i=j</math> are not considered) which correspond to time intervals (or time lags) <math>\,\Delta t_{ij} = (j - i)\,\Delta t</math>. Hence, there are many distinct displacements for small time lags, and very few for large time lags, <math>{\rm MSD}</math> can be defined as an average quantity over time lags:<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Michalet |first1=Xavier |title=Mean square displacement analysis of single-particle trajectories with localization error: Brownian motion in an isotropic medium |journal=Physical Review E |date=20 October 2010 |volume=82 |issue=4 |article-number=041914 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevE.82.041914 |pmid=21230320 |pmc=3055791 |bibcode=2010PhRvE..82d1914M }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Qian |first1=H. |last2=Sheetz |first2=M. P. |last3=Elson |first3=E. L. |title=Single particle tracking. Analysis of diffusion and flow in two-dimensional systems |journal=Biophysical Journal |date=1 October 1991 |volume=60 |issue=4 |pages=910–921 |doi=10.1016/S0006-3495(91)82125-7 |pmid=1742458 |pmc=1260142 |bibcode=1991BpJ....60..910Q |language=en |issn=0006-3495}}</ref>

<math display="block">\overline{\delta^2(n)} =\frac 1 {N-n} \sum_{i = 1}^{N - n} {(\vec r_{i + n} - \vec r_i} )^2 \qquad n=1,\ldots,N-1.</math>

Similarly, for continuous [[time series]] :

<math display="block">\overline {\delta^2(\Delta )} = \frac 1 {T - \Delta} \int_0^{T - \Delta} [r(t + \Delta ) - r(t)]^2 \, dt </math>

It's clear that choosing large <math>T</math> and <math>\Delta \ll T</math> can improve statistical performance. This technique allow us estimate the behavior of the whole ensembles by just measuring a single trajectory, but note that it's only valid for the systems with [[ergodicity]], like classical [[Brownian motion]] (BM), [[fractional Brownian motion]] (fBM), and [[continuous-time random walk]] (CTRW) with limited distribution of waiting times, in these cases, <math>\overline {\delta^2(\Delta)} = \left\langle [r(t) - r(0)]^2 \right\rangle </math> (defined above), here <math>\left\langle \cdot \right\rangle </math> denotes ensembles average. However, for non-ergodic systems, like the CTRW with unlimited waiting time, waiting time can go to infinity at some time, in this case, <math>\overline {\delta^2(\Delta )}</math> strongly depends on <math>T</math>, <math>\overline{\delta^2(\Delta)}</math> and <math> \left\langle [r(t) - r(0)]^2 \right\rangle </math> don't equal each other anymore, in order to get better asymptotics, introduce the averaged time MSD:

<math display="block">\left\langle {\overline{\delta^2(\Delta)} } \right\rangle = \frac{1}{N} \sum \overline {\delta^2(\Delta)} </math>

Here <math>\left\langle \cdot \right\rangle </math> denotes averaging over ''N'' ensembles. 

Also, one can easily derive the autocorrelation function from the MSD:

<math display="block">\left\langle {[r(t) - r(0)]^2} \right\rangle = \left\langle r^2(t) \right\rangle + \left\langle r^2(0) \right\rangle - 2\left\langle r(t)r(0) \right\rangle, </math>where <math> \left\langle r(t)r(0) \right\rangle </math> is so-called [[autocorrelation]] function for position of particles.

==MSD in experiments==
Experimental methods to determine MSDs include [[neutron scattering]] and [[photon correlation spectroscopy]].

The linear relationship between the MSD and time ''t'' allows for graphical methods to determine the diffusivity constant ''D''. This is especially useful for rough calculations of the diffusivity in environmental systems. In some [[Atmospheric dispersion modeling|atmospheric dispersion models]], the relationship between MSD and time ''t'' is not linear. Instead, a series of power laws empirically representing the variation of the square root of MSD versus downwind distance are commonly used in studying the dispersion phenomenon.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Davidson|first=G. A.|date=1990-08-01|title=A Modified Power Law Representation of the Pasquill-Gifford Dispersion Coefficients|journal=Journal of the Air & Waste Management Association|volume=40|issue=8|pages=1146–1147|doi=10.1080/10473289.1990.10466761|issn=1047-3289}}</ref>
